title: Festivals and everyday culture
job: Talk about what is happening around you
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: kotóryy IS THE MODULE, and it is the most useful single word in the level: a festival nobody in your family has heard of cannot be described without a relative clause. Its law has two halves and both matter. It agrees in GENDER and NUMBER with the noun it points back at — prázdnik, kotóryy … but kníga, kotóraya … — and it takes its CASE from its own clause, not from that noun. kníga, kotóruyu ya chitál has a feminine word in the accusative because the reading, not the book, decides.

The comma in front of kotóryy is obligatory, which is M3's law for the third time in this level. By now it should be predictable rather than surprising: Russian marks the seam between clauses with a comma every time, whether the second clause opens with chto, yésli or kotóryy, and there is no case in which leaving it out is acceptable.

DATES take the genitive twice over: pérvogo yanvaryá, vos'mógo márta, devyátogo máya — an ordinal in the genitive and a month in the genitive, with no preposition at all where English needs "on" and "of". The naming form is different: pérvoye yanvaryá is the date as a label, and pérvogo yanvaryá is the date as a when. Months are written in lower case, which an English habit will fight.

na takes the ACCUSATIVE for a festival you go to and the prepositional for one you are already at — L2-M4's contrast, in a new field: na Nóvyy god, na den' rozhdéniya. byváyet is the other half of the module's grammar of the year: it means "there tends to be", the thing that happens in that month most years, and it never changes for the person because it has no person.

The festival names are learnt WHOLE, as one word each: Nóvyy god, den' rozhdéniya, Den' Pobédy. Taking them apart is a waste of effort — god on its own is a year, and den' rozhdéniya translates literally as "day of birth", which nobody needs to know to use it. yólka is the New Year tree, and it arrives at New Year rather than at Christmas.

sentences.cue: It's a holiday that I love

words.note: A public holiday or a celebration, not a holiday from work — that one is ótpusk. The d is silent: PRAZ-nik.
The relative word. Masculine here because prázdnik is masculine, and nominative because it is the subject of its own clause. Plural: kotórye.

sentences.trap: English drops "that" as often as not. Russian never drops kotóryy, and never drops the comma in front of it.
sentences.sound: EH-ta PRAZ-nik, ka-TO-ryy ya lyub-LYU. No d in prázdnik at all.

variations.cue: These are holidays that I love

variations.display: Éhto prázdnik, kotóryy ya ne lyublyú
variations.script: Это праздник, который я не люблю
variations.cue: It's a holiday I don't like

mistake.why: Two clauses have been run together with nothing between them. Russian needs kotóryy and the comma before it.

sentences.usage: Explaining a date in your diary to somebody who does not know it.
sentences.mnemonic: kotóryy takes its gender from behind and its case from in front.

sentences.display: Na Nóvyy god my poydyóm v kafé
sentences.script: На Новый год мы пойдём в кафе
sentences.cue: At New Year we'll go to a café
sentences.literal: On New Year we will-go into café

words.note: The biggest holiday of the Russian year, learnt as one word. na plus the accusative is what you say for going to it — and the accusative happens to look like the plain form.

sentences.trap: na and not v for a festival. v Nóvyy god would put you inside the year rather than at the celebration.
sentences.sound: na NO-vyy got my pay-DYOM f ka-FE. The d of god is said as a t, and the v of v kafé as an f.

variations.cue: At New Year we're at home
variations.changed: staying in, with no verb at all

variations.display: Na Nóvyy god my poydyóm k sestré
variations.script: На Новый год мы пойдём к сестре
variations.cue: At New Year we'll go to my sister's

mistake.display: V Nóvyy god my poydyóm v kafé
mistake.script: В Новый год мы пойдём в кафе
mistake.why: A festival takes na. v is for the place you walk into, which is why kafé keeps it in the same sentence.

sentences.usage: Making plans for the one night of the year everybody has plans for.
sentences.mnemonic: na the festival, v the café.

sentences.cue: On the first of January we're at home

words.note: The genitive of the ordinal, which is how Russian says "on the Nth". The label form is pérvoye: pérvoye yanvaryá is the date, pérvogo yanvaryá is the day it happens on.
January in the genitive, which every date needs. The plain name is yanvár' and "in January" is v yanvaré — and it is written in lower case, always.

sentences.trap: No preposition anywhere. English has "on" and "of" and Russian has two genitive endings doing the work of both.
sentences.sound: PYER-va-va yan-va-RYA my DO-ma. The -ogo ending is said -ava, as it is everywhere else.

variations.cue: On the first of March we're at home
The first of January is a holiday
variations.changed: the date as a label, so pérvoye

mistake.why: There is no v in a date, and both words take the genitive: pérvogo yanvaryá.

sentences.usage: Saying when something falls, which is half of every arrangement.
sentences.mnemonic: Two genitives and no preposition — that is a Russian date.

sentences.cue: On the eighth of March I bought a present

words.note: The eighth, in the same genitive as pérvogo. Vos'móye márta is a holiday in its own right — Women's Day — and it is a day on which presents are expected.
March in the genitive, for dates. The plain name is mart and "in March" is v márte. Lower case, like every month.

sentences.trap: podárok is L1-M6's row and has not changed. What is new here is only the date in front of it.
sentences.sound: vas-MO-va MAR-ta ya ku-PIL pa-DA-rak. The soft sign in vos'mógo is a tiny pause, not a vowel.

variations.cue: On the eighth of March I bought a present
The eighth of March is a holiday

mistake.why: That is the label form, and it can only name the day. The day something happened on is vos'mógo.

sentences.usage: The one date in the Russian year that guarantees queues at the florist.
sentences.mnemonic: -ogo for when, -oye for what it is called.

sentences.cue: It tends to be cold in January

words.cue: tends to be, happens to be
words.note: Not "is" but "is usually" — what happens in that month most years. It has no person and never agrees with anybody; the plural of the thing makes it byváyut.

sentences.trap: byváyet is the habit and not the day. For the weather this morning you would say nothing at all: khólodno on its own.
sentences.sound: v yan-va-RYE by-VA-yet KHO-lad-na. The v at the front is a single consonant on the month.

variations.cue: It tends to be cold in March
It gets hot here
variations.changed: a place instead of a month

mistake.why: "In a month" takes the prepositional: v yanvaré. The plain yanvár' is only the name of it.

sentences.usage: Warning a visitor about the month they have chosen.
sentences.mnemonic: byváyet — the way it usually is, not the way it is today.

sentences.cue: This is the book I was reading

words.note: Both halves of the law in one word: feminine because kníga is, accusative because it is what the reading was done to. The subject form would be kotóraya.

sentences.trap: The case does NOT come from kníga. It comes from the second clause, where the book is the object.
sentences.sound: EH-ta KNI-ga, ka-TO-ru-yu ya chi-TAL. kotóruyu is four syllables and only the second is stressed.

variations.cue: This is the book I bought
variations.changed: a different verb in the clause

variations.cue: This is the paper I was reading

mistake.why: kotóraya is the subject form, and the book is not doing the reading. What is read takes the accusative: kotóruyu.

sentences.usage: Handing something over and saying what it is.
sentences.mnemonic: Gender from the noun behind, case from the clause ahead.

sentences.cue: This is the letter I wrote

words.note: The neuter form, for words like pis'mó and soobshchéniye. Its accusative looks exactly like its nominative, which is true of every neuter noun as well.

sentences.trap: Neuter hides the case, since the two forms are identical. The rule is still doing its work — you simply cannot see it here.
sentences.sound: EH-ta pis-MO, ka-TO-ra-ye ya na-pi-SAL. The final -oye is said -aye.

variations.cue: This is the letter I read
This is the message I wrote

mistake.why: pis'mó is neuter, so the relative word has to be too: kotóroye.

sentences.usage: Showing somebody the thing you have just been talking about.
sentences.mnemonic: pis'mó is neuter, so kotóroye follows it.

words.note: Two words, one item of vocabulary: keep it whole. It is masculine, because den' is, which is why it takes moy rather than moyá.

sentences.trap: No verb in the sentence and none missing. "Is" has no present tense in Russian.
sentences.sound: moy dyen razh-DYE-ni-ya v MAR-tye. rozhdéniya runs together into three quick syllables.

variations.cue: My birthday is in January

variations.display: Na den' rozhdéniya my býli v kafé
variations.script: На день рождения мы были в кафе
variations.cue: For the birthday we were at a café
variations.changed: na plus the festival, in the past

mistake.why: den' is masculine and carries the whole phrase with it, so the possessive is moy.

sentences.usage: The answer to the question every new colleague asks in the first week.
sentences.mnemonic: den' rozhdéniya — one word in two pieces, and masculine.

sentences.cue: The ninth of May is Victory Day

words.note: The ninth, in the date genitive again. The pattern is fixed by now: the ordinal ends in -ogo and the month follows it in the genitive.
May in the genitive. The plain name is may — one syllable, and the shortest month name in the language.
The ninth of May, and the largest public holiday after Nóvyy god. Learnt whole, like every festival name here.

sentences.trap: The dash stands where English puts "is". It is written, and in speech it is a pause.
sentences.sound: di-VYA-ta-va MA-ya, dyen pa-BYE-dy. A clear pause where the dash is.

variations.cue: The ninth of May is a holiday
variations.changed: the label form of the date

variations.cue: On Victory Day we're at home

mistake.why: Both forms exist and this one names the date rather than placing an event on it. As a label it is fine; as "on the ninth" it must be devyátogo.

sentences.usage: Explaining the calendar to someone who has just arrived.
sentences.mnemonic: Ninth of May, whole and unchanged: Den' Pobédy.

sentences.cue: I bought a New Year tree

words.note: The tree that goes up for Nóvyy god rather than for Christmas. Accusative after kupíl; standing in the corner it is a yólka.

sentences.trap: It arrives in December for the New Year. Calling it a Christmas tree misses the holiday it belongs to.
sentences.sound: ya ku-PIL YOL-ku. The yo is always stressed — that letter is never unstressed in Russian.

variations.cue: I bought a New Year tree
I bought a tree and a present

mistake.why: What is bought takes the accusative, and for a feminine noun that means -u: yólku.

sentences.usage: Late December, and the boot of the car.
sentences.mnemonic: The yo is stressed, and the tree is for the New Year.
